title: Noise in Circuits
intro: Because the noise of a circuit depends on its gain, designers refer all noise to the input so that stages can be compared with the signal.

blocks.text: Divide the output noise PSD by the squared gain to get an equivalent noise source at the input that would produce the same output if the circuit were noiseless. It is the number to compare with the minimum signal you need to detect.

The transistor contributes 4kT*gamma/gm, and the load resistor contributes a term that falls with gm^2*RD, i.e. with gain. To lower input noise, raise gm: it also raises gain. But gm costs current, so low noise costs power.

Since thermal input noise is proportional to 1/gm and gm is proportional to the square root of current at fixed W/L, halving the noise power needs twice the gm: four times the current at a fixed W/L, or twice the current (with twice the width) at a fixed Vov. Low-noise design is therefore a power negotiation.

items: Common-gate and follower: the same transistor noise 4kT*gamma/gm appears at the input, plus a term from the load resistor; they are rarely used when noise matters.
Cascode: the upper device contributes little because the lower device's drain resistance is so high; noise is close to the CS stage.
Current mirrors and differential pairs: each transistor adds its noise. In a pair with mirror load, load transistors add gm3/gm1 times their share. Make gm of the load smaller than the input pair's.

blocks.text: To compare a real filter or amplifier with an ideal one, define the noise bandwidth as the width of a brick-wall filter with the same total noise. For a single-pole filter with pole at fp, the noise bandwidth is (pi/2)*fp = 1.57*fp, a little above the -3 dB bandwidth.

blocks.title: CS stage input noise
blocks.text: gm = 2 mS, RD = 10 kohm, gamma = 2/3. Find the input-referred thermal noise density at 300 K.
blocks.answer: About 2.4 nV/sqrt(Hz), mostly from the transistor.

blocks.title: Integrated noise
blocks.text: White noise of 10 nV/sqrt(Hz) is applied to a one-pole low-pass filter with pole at 1 MHz. Find the total rms output noise.
